title: Systemic Anatomy I: The Skeletal System

content.text: The skeletal system consists of 206 bones in the adult human body. Bones provide structural support, protection of internal organs, movement (serve as levers for muscles), mineral storage (calcium, phosphorus), and blood cell formation (hematopoiesis in bone marrow). Bones are classified by shape: long bones (femur, humerus), short bones (carpals), flat bones (cranium, sternum), irregular bones (vertebrae), and sesamoid bones (patella).

content.text: Bones consist of compact (dense) bone on the outside and spongy (cancellous) bone on the inside. The periosteum is a fibrous membrane covering the outer surface. The endosteum lines the inner surface. Bone cells include osteoblasts (bone-forming), osteocytes (mature bone cells), and osteoclasts (bone-destroying). The bone matrix is composed of organic components (collagen fibers, proteoglycans) for flexibility and inorganic mineral salts (hydroxyapatite, calcium phosphate) for hardness and strength.

content.text: Bones develop through two processes: Intramembranous ossification (bones develop directly from mesenchymal tissue, e.g., cranial bones) and Endochondral ossification (bones develop from cartilage models, e.g., long bones). Bone growth occurs at the epiphyseal plates in growing children. Bone remodeling is the continuous process of bone resorption and formation, regulated by hormones (growth hormone, estrogen, testosterone) and mechanical stress.

content.text: The axial skeleton (80 bones) includes the skull, vertebral column, rib cage, and sternum. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) includes the pectoral girdle (clavicles, scapulae), upper limbs (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges), pelvic girdle (hip bones), and lower limbs (femur, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges).

content.text: Joints are where two or more bones meet. Joints are classified by structure: Fibrous joints (sutures of the skull, immovable), Cartilaginous joints (pubic symphysis, slightly movable), and Synovial joints (freely movable, contain synovial fluid). Types of synovial joints include: Ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), Hinge (elbow, knee), Pivot (atlantoaxial), Condyloid (wrist), Saddle (thumb), and Gliding (carpals).
